name_en: An inner product assigns a unique real number, for all x, y, z and all real scalars c
name_zh: 内积给出唯一实数,并对所有 x, y, z 与所有实标量 c 成立
statement: The framing clause of the definition: an inner product on a real linear space V is a map that assigns to each pair x, y in V one and only one REAL number (x, y), and the axioms are required for all x, y, z in V and all real scalars c. Two things are fixed here before any axiom is stated: the value is real, and the axioms are universally quantified rather than asserted for special elements. The reality of the value is exactly what must be relaxed in the complex case.

anchors.quote: DEFINITION. A real linear space V is said to have an inner product if for each pair of elements x and y in V there corresponds a unique real
satisfying the following axioms for all choices of x, y, z in V and all real scalars c.

atomic_reason: It is a single well-definedness-plus-quantifier clause; splitting it further would separate 'unique' from 'real number' from 'for all', which are not independently usable mathematical contents.

name_en: The inner product is defined axiomatically, not by a formula
name_zh: 内积是公理式定义,而非由公式定义
statement: Apostol defines the inner product by listing properties and declaring them axioms, instead of prescribing a formula such as the component sum. This is the methodological pivot of 15.10: every later theorem (15.8, 15.9, 15.10-15.12) is then a consequence of the axioms alone and therefore holds in every model, including function spaces where no component sum exists.

anchors.quote: we define the product axiomatically rather than by a specific formula
The reader should verify that each of the following satisfies all the axioms for an inner product.

atomic_reason: A single methodological commitment with no independent sub-parts; it is either adopted or not.

name_en: Axiom 1: symmetry (commutativity) of the real inner product
name_zh: 公理1:实内积的对称性(交换性)
statement: Axiom (1): (x, y) = (y, x) for all x, y. What it forbids: any product that distinguishes the order of its arguments. Dropping only this axiom leaves a form linear in the second variable but with no transfer of that linearity to the first variable, so (x + y, z) can no longer be expanded, the expansion (x+y, x+y) = (x,x) + (y,y) + (x,y) + (y,x) used for the triangle inequality collapses, and the step 'pair the equation with x_1' in Theorems 15.10 and 15.11 becomes unavailable.

anchors.quote: (1) $(x,y) = (y,x)$ (commutativity, or symmetry).

atomic_reason: A single equation between two expressions, with no conjunction, case split, or quantifier structure that could be separated further.

name_en: Axiom 2: additivity (distributivity) in the second argument
name_zh: 公理2:对第二个变元的可加性(分配性)
statement: Axiom (2): (x, y + z) = (x, y) + (x, z) for all x, y, z. Apostol states additivity in the SECOND slot only; additivity in the first slot is not an axiom but a consequence of (2) together with symmetry. What it forbids: any product that fails to split a sum in its second argument. Dropping only this axiom kills every 'pair the identity with a basis element and expand the sum' argument, i.e. the proofs of Theorem 15.10, Theorem 15.11 and Parseval's formula.

anchors.quote: (2) $(x,y + z) = (x,y) + (x,z)$ (distributivity, or linearity).

atomic_reason: One equation in one slot; the companion statement for the other slot is a separate derived node rather than a part of this one.

name_en: Axiom 3: homogeneity in the first argument
name_zh: 公理3:对第一个变元的齐次性
statement: Axiom (3): c(x, y) = (cx, y) for every scalar c. What it forbids: any product on which scalars cannot be pulled out of the first slot. Dropping only this axiom destroys the norm identity ||cx|| = |c| ||x|| (Theorem 15.9c), the extraction of the coefficients c_i in the proofs of Theorems 15.10 and 15.11, and the corollary (O, y) = 0. Because the display of axiom (3) occupies a line of only 21 characters, the anchor below is the sentence that names the axiom and uses it.

anchors.quote: Note: Taking $c = 0$ in (3), we find that $(O, y) = 0$ for all $y$ .
In the homogeneity axiom, the scalar multiplier c can be any complex number.

atomic_reason: One equation relating a scalar multiple of the value to the value at a scalar multiple; no further independent content.

name_en: Axiom 4: strict positivity, (x, x) > 0 if x is not the zero element
name_zh: 公理4:严格正定性,x 非零时 (x, x) > 0
statement: The fourth axiom: (x, x) > 0 whenever x is not the zero element. What it forbids: semi-definite forms. If the strict inequality is weakened to (x, x) >= 0, one gets a positive SEMI-definite form on which there may exist nonzero elements with (x, x) = 0, hence nonzero elements of norm zero. Then Theorem 15.9(b) fails, ||x|| = 0 no longer characterizes x = O, the angle quotient (x,y)/(||x|| ||y||) can have zero denominator for nonzero arguments, the step '(x_1, x_1) is not 0 since x_1 is not O' in Theorem 15.10 fails, and the denominator (e_j, e_j) in Theorem 15.11 may vanish.

anchors.quote: (x, x) > 0 \quad i f \quad x \neq O

atomic_reason: A single strict inequality under a single hypothesis; no conjunction to split.

name_en: The zero element has zero inner product with everything
name_zh: 零元与任何元素的内积为零
statement: Taking c = 0 in the homogeneity axiom (3) gives (O, y) = 0 for all y. This is Apostol's own remark. It is what makes the zero element orthogonal to every element in 15.11, and it is used implicitly whenever a vanishing linear combination is paired with a basis element.

anchors.quote: Note: Taking $c = 0$ in (3), we find that $(O, y) = 0$ for all $y$ .

atomic_reason: A one-line corollary obtained by a single substitution c = 0; there is no intermediate step to expose.

name_en: Additivity in the first argument is derived, not assumed
name_zh: 对第一个变元的可加性是推论,不是公理
statement: (x + y, z) = (x, z) + (y, z) is NOT one of Apostol's axioms. It follows by using symmetry (1) to swap into the second slot, applying additivity (2) there, and swapping back. This is the precise reason the symmetry axiom is load-bearing in the proofs: the expansion (x + y, x + y) = (x, x) + (y, y) + (x, y) + (y, x) that opens the proof of the triangle inequality, and the step 'pair the vanishing combination with x_1' in Theorem 15.10, both split a sum in the FIRST slot, which axiom (2) alone does not license.

anchors.quote: (2) $(x,y + z) = (x,y) + (x,z)$ (distributivity, or linearity).

origin_note: Apostol does not spell out this derivation; the two anchors give the axiom he does state and the computation that silently uses the first-slot version. The derivation itself is supplied by this node.
atomic_reason: A single identity obtained by one symmetry-swap sandwich around axiom (2); no separable sub-claim.

name_en: Axiom 1': Hermitian symmetry replaces symmetry in a complex space
name_zh: 公理1':复空间中 Hermite 对称取代对称性
statement: In a complex linear space the symmetry axiom (1) is replaced by (x, y) = conjugate of (y, x), labelled (1') by Apostol. Every other axiom is kept verbatim. What it forbids: plain symmetry, which in the complex case is incompatible with strict positivity, since plain symmetry plus complex homogeneity in the first slot would force (cx, cx) = c^2 (x, x) and thus a negative or non-real value of (x, x) for suitable c.

anchors.quote: cept that the symmetry axiom is replaced by the relation
(x, y) = \overline {{(y , x)}},\tag{1'}
where $(y, x)$ denotes the complex conjugate of $(y, x)$ .

atomic_reason: One equation replacing one equation; the reason it is forced is recorded as a separate consequence node.

name_en: In the complex case the homogeneity scalar may be any complex number
name_zh: 复情形下齐次性公理中的标量可取任意复数
statement: The second modification Apostol makes: in axiom (3) the multiplier c is allowed to be any complex number, not merely a real one. This widening is what turns the replacement of (1) by (1') into a chain reaction, because it is the combination 'complex c in the first slot' plus 'conjugation on swapping slots' that produces conjugate-homogeneity in the second slot.

anchors.quote: In the homogeneity axiom, the scalar multiplier c can be any complex number.

atomic_reason: A single widening of the scalar range in a single axiom.

name_en: Companion relation: (x, cy) = conjugate(c) (x, y)
name_zh: 配套关系:(x, cy) = c 的共轭乘 (x, y)
statement: Apostol's 'companion relation', obtained from the homogeneity axiom together with (1'): (x, cy) = conjugate of (cy, x) = conjugate(c) times conjugate of (y, x) = conjugate(c) (x, y). This is the exact point at which changing the symmetry axiom propagates into the homogeneity behaviour: homogeneity is left untouched in the first slot but becomes CONJUGATE homogeneity in the second slot. Nothing about slot two was postulated; it is forced.

anchors.quote: From the homogeneity axiom and $(1')$ , we get
(x, c y) = \overline {{(c y , x)}} = \bar {c} (\overline {{y , x}}) = \bar {c} (x, y).

atomic_reason: Apostol displays the derivation as three equalities in one line; each equality is a single application of an axiom already held as its own node, so no further split adds content.

name_en: Hermitian symmetry makes (x, x) real, so the positivity axiom still parses
name_zh: Hermite 对称使 (x, x) 为实数,正定性公理才有意义
statement: Setting y = x in (1') gives (x, x) = conjugate of (x, x), so (x, x) is real. This is the hidden step that lets the unchanged positivity axiom '(x, x) > 0 if x is not O' remain meaningful in a complex space, where the inequality sign would otherwise be applied to a non-real number. It is also why (1') and not plain symmetry is the correct replacement.

anchors.quote: In a complex linear space, an inner product $(x, y)$ is a complex number satisfying the same axioms as those for a real inner produ
(x, y) = \overline {{(y , x)}},\tag{1'}

origin_note: Apostol says the other axioms are kept unchanged but never remarks that (1') is what makes (x, x) real. The anchors give his statement of (1') and of 'same axioms'; the deduction y = x is supplied here.
atomic_reason: A one-substitution consequence (y := x) of a single axiom.

name_en: In a complex space (x, y)(y, x) equals the modulus squared
name_zh: 复空间中 (x, y)(y, x) 等于模的平方
statement: When the real proof is run in a complex Euclidean space it yields (x, y)(y, x) <= (x, x)(y, y). Apostol closes the gap by the identity (x, y)(y, x) = (x, y) times conjugate of (x, y) = |(x, y)|^2, which uses (1') alone. This single line is what makes one statement of Theorem 15.8 cover both the real and the complex case.

anchors.quote: When we apply this proof in a complex Euclidean space, we obtain the inequality $(x, y)(y, x) \leq (x, x)(y, y)$ , which is the same as the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality since

atomic_reason: One two-step identity, each step a single use of (1') and of z times conjugate z = |z|^2.

name_en: Unqualified 'Euclidean space' means real or complex
name_zh: 未加限定的「欧几里得空间」兼指实与复两种情形
statement: A reading convention with mathematical force: whenever Apostol writes 'Euclidean space' without further designation, the space may be real or complex, and every theorem of the chapter is asserted for both. This is why Theorem 15.8, 15.9, 15.10, 15.11 and 15.12 must be read as complex statements too, and why conjugates appear in the proof of the triangle inequality and in Parseval's formula.

anchors.quote: en we use the term Euclidean space without further designation, it is to be understood that the space can be real or complex.
theorems of this chapter are valid for complex Euclidean spaces as well.

atomic_reason: A single scoping convention; it cannot be decomposed without losing its function.

name_en: Metric properties are the target; the inner product is the means
name_zh: 度量性质是目标,内积是手段
statement: The organizing motive of 15.10: properties that rely on measuring lengths of segments and angles between lines are called metric properties; in V_n both were defined via the dot product; so to obtain them in a general linear space one first generalizes the dot product to an inner product and only then defines length and angle in terms of it. This fixes the dependency order inner product -> norm -> angle that the rest of the section follows.

anchors.quote: those properties that rely on the possibility of measuring lengths of line segments and angles between lines are called metric properti
In our study of $V_{n}$ , we defined lengths and angles in terms of the dot product
We shall introduce first a generalization of the dot product, which we call an inner product, and then define length and angle in terms of the inner product.

atomic_reason: A single ordering decision (product first, then length and angle); its two consequences are already separate nodes (norm, angle).

name_en: A linear space can carry more than one inner product
name_zh: 同一线性空间上可有多个内积
statement: Example 2 exhibits on V_2 the form (x, y) = 2x_1y_1 + x_1y_2 + x_2y_1 + x_2y_2, which satisfies all the axioms yet differs from the dot product. Apostol draws the conclusion explicitly: there may be more than one inner product in a given linear space. Hence 'Euclidean space' is a linear space together with a chosen inner product, not a property of the linear space alone.

anchors.quote: This example shows that there may be more than one inner product in a given linear space.

atomic_reason: One existence statement backed by one explicit example; no sub-parts.

name_en: The dot product as the component sum (Equation 15.5)
name_zh: 点积作为分量之和(式 15.5)
statement: Equation (15.5): x . y is the sum over i from 1 to n of x_i y_i, for x and y in V_n. This concrete formula is the object that the axioms abstract from; the integral inner product on C(a, b) is built by the same pattern with function values for components and integration for summation.

anchors.quote: x \cdot y = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} x _ {i} y _ {i}.\tag{15.5}

atomic_reason: A single closed formula; the summand and the summation are not independent mathematical contents.

name_en: The dot product on V_n is an inner product (Example 1)
name_zh: V_n 上的点积是一个内积(例 1)
statement: Example 1: taking (x, y) = x . y in V_n satisfies all four axioms, so V_n with the dot product is a real Euclidean space. This is the verification that the axiom system is non-vacuous and that the generalization really contains its model.

anchors.quote: EXAMPLE 1. In $V_{n}$ let $(x, y) = x \cdot y$ , the usual dot product of $x$ and $y$ .
The reader should verify that each of the following satisfies all the axioms for an inner product.

atomic_reason: One model-checking claim; the four axiom verifications are routine component computations, not further mathematical content in this chapter.

name_en: The integral inner product on C(a, b)
name_zh: C(a, b) 上的积分内积
statement: Example 3 defines, on the space of real-valued functions continuous on [a, b], the inner product (f, g) = integral from a to b of f(t)g(t) dt. This is the first model of the axioms in which the elements are not tuples, and it is the model Apostol uses to turn Theorem 15.8 into an inequality about integrals.

anchors.quote: EXAMPLE 3. Let $C(a, b)$ denote the linear space of all real-valued functions continuous on an interval $[a, b]$ .
(f, g) = \int_ {a} ^ {b} f (t) g (t) d t.

atomic_reason: A single closed formula defining one bilinear form.

name_en: Function values play the role of components, integration the role of summation
name_zh: 函数值充当分量,积分充当求和
statement: Apostol states the structural analogy explicitly: the integral formula is analogous to (15.5), with f(t) and g(t) in the role of the components x_i and y_i, and integration in the role of summation. This is the bridge that justifies calling the axiomatic notion a generalization of the dot product rather than an unrelated abstraction, and it is the reason positive definiteness holds (the integral of f^2 is positive for a continuous f that is not identically zero).

anchors.quote: This formula is analogous to Equation (15.5) which defines the dot product of two vectors in $V_{n}$ .
The function values $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ play the role of the components $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ , and integration takes the place of summation.

atomic_reason: A single two-part correspondence stated in one sentence; the two halves (values-for-components, integral-for-sum) are not separately usable.

name_en: The weight function must be a fixed positive continuous function
name_zh: 权函数必须是固定的正连续函数
statement: In Example 4 the weighted form (f, g) = integral of w(t)f(t)g(t) dt is an inner product only because w is a FIXED POSITIVE function in C(a, b). Positivity of w is exactly what carries the positive definiteness axiom: if w were allowed to change sign or vanish on a subinterval, (f, f) could be zero or negative for some nonzero continuous f, and axiom (4) would fail while axioms (1)-(3) would still hold. Example 3 is the special case w(t) = 1.

anchors.quote: (f, g) = \int_ {a} ^ {b} w (t) f (t) g (t) d t,
where w is a fixed positive function in $C(a, b)$ . The function w is called a weight function. In Example 3 we have $w(t) = 1$ for all t.

atomic_reason: A single hypothesis on a single function; its role in axiom (4) is recorded as a requires edge rather than a sub-node.

name_en: On polynomials, the exponential weight secures convergence
name_zh: 多项式空间上,指数权保证反常积分收敛
statement: Example 5 puts (f, g) = integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-t) f(t) g(t) dt on the space of all real polynomials. Apostol points out that the exponential factor is what makes this improper integral converge for every choice of polynomials. Here the weight does double duty: positivity gives axiom (4), and decay gives well-definedness of the value at all, which on an unbounded interval is a prerequisite for the axioms even to be checkable.

anchors.quote: (f, g) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- t} f (t) g (t) d t.
Because of the exponential factor, this improper integral converges for every choice of polynomials f and g.

atomic_reason: One convergence observation about one specific integral.

name_en: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality proper: |(x, y)|^2 <= (x, x)(y, y)
name_zh: Cauchy-Schwarz 不等式本体:|(x, y)|^2 <= (x, x)(y, y)
statement: The inequality clause of Theorem 15.8: in a Euclidean space, every inner product satisfies |(x, y)|^2 <= (x, x)(y, y) for all x and y in V. This clause alone needs no strict positivity: the standard argument bounds the quantity (x - ty, x - ty) >= 0, so positive SEMI-definiteness suffices to obtain the inequality. Strict positivity is needed only for the equality clause.

anchors.quote: THEOREM 15.8. In a Euclidean space V, every inner product satisfies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality:
| (x, y) | ^ {2} \leq (x, x) (y, y) \quad f o r a l l x a n d y i n V.

atomic_reason: A single inequality between two products; nothing separable remains once the equality clause is split off.

name_en: Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz holds if and only if x and y are dependent
name_zh: Cauchy-Schwarz 取等号当且仅当 x 与 y 相依
statement: The second clause of Theorem 15.8, and the only biconditional in the section: |(x, y)|^2 = (x, x)(y, y) exactly when the set {x, y} is dependent. For nonzero x and y dependence means y = cx, and then the angle between them is 0 if c > 0 and pi if c < 0, so the cosine attains an endpoint of [-1, 1]; if x = O or y = O the set is dependent and equality holds, but the pair has no angle at all under the definition of 15.10. It is here, and only here, that STRICT positivity is required: semi-definiteness would still give the inequality, but with (z, z) = 0 possible for z not O one could have equality without x - ty = O, so dependence could not be concluded.

anchors.quote: Moreover, the equality sign holds if and only if x and y are dependent.

atomic_reason: One biconditional characterization; its two directions share a single proof and are not separately stated by Apostol.

name_en: The proof is inherited: it used only the properties in Theorem 12.2
name_zh: 证明是继承而来的:它只用到定理 12.2 所列性质
statement: Apostol's proof strategy for 15.8 is a re-use argument, not a new computation. In proving the V_n case (Theorem 12.3) he was careful that the proof drew only on the properties of the dot product listed in Theorem 12.2, never on the component formula. Because those listed properties are precisely the inner-product axioms, the identical proof runs in any real Euclidean space. This is the paradigm of the whole section: axiomatize the properties actually used, and every theorem transfers for free.

anchors.quote: the proof was a consequence of the properties of the dot product listed in Theorem 12.2 and did not depend on the particular definition used to deduce these properties
Therefore, the very same proof is valid in any real Euclidean space.

atomic_reason: Not atomic: the inherited proof itself has internal steps (form (x - ty, x - ty) >= 0, expand, optimize in t), but those steps live in Chapter 12, outside the two source files for this subtree, so they cannot be anchored here and are deliberately left unexpanded.

name_en: Cauchy-Schwarz in norm form: |(x, y)| <= ||x|| ||y||
name_zh: Cauchy-Schwarz 的范数形式:|(x, y)| <= ||x|| ||y||

anchors.quote: When the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is expressed in terms of norms, it becomes

atomic_reason: A single restatement obtained by one square-root step from a node already held.

name_en: Cauchy-Schwarz applied to C(a, b) gives the integral inequality
name_zh: Cauchy-Schwarz 用于 C(a, b) 得到积分不等式
statement: Instantiating Theorem 15.8 in C(a, b) with the integral inner product yields (integral of fg)^2 <= (integral of f^2)(integral of g^2). Apostol offers it as the pay-off of the axiomatic route: a nontrivial analytic inequality obtained with no new work, purely by checking that the integral form satisfies the axioms.

anchors.quote: EXAMPLE. Applying Theorem 15.8 to the space $C(a, b)$ with the inner product $(f, g) = \int_{a}^{b} f(t) g(t) dt$ , we find that the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality becomes
\left(\int_ {a} ^ {b} f (t) g (t) d t\right) ^ {2} \leq \left(\int_ {a} ^ {b} f ^ {2} (t) d t\right) \left(\int_ {a} ^ {b} g ^ {2} (t) d t\right).

atomic_reason: One instantiation of one theorem in one model; no intermediate step exists.

name_en: The norm is defined as the square root of (x, x)
name_zh: 范数定义为 (x, x) 的平方根
statement: Definition: in a Euclidean space V the nonnegative number ||x|| = (x, x)^(1/2) is called the norm of x. Two things are asserted at once and both rest on axioms: that the number under the root is nonnegative, so the real square root exists, and that the nonnegative branch is the one taken, so ||x|| >= 0 by construction rather than by proof.

anchors.quote: DEFINITION. In a Euclidean space V, the nonnegative number $\|x\|$ defined by the equation
is called the norm of the element $x$ .

name_en: Theorem 15.9 quantifies over all elements, all scalars, and every norm
name_zh: 定理 15.9 对一切元素、一切标量、每个范数成立
statement: The framing clause of Theorem 15.9: in a Euclidean space, EVERY norm has properties (a)-(d) for ALL elements x and y and ALL scalars c. Combined with the fact that a space may carry several inner products, this is the exact content of the theorem's significance: (a)-(d) are the properties that survive any choice of inner product, and they are therefore the right axioms for a norm in the abstract.

anchors.quote: THEOREM 15.9. In a Euclidean space, every norm has the following properties for all elements $x$ and $y$ and all scalars $c$ :

name_zh: 性质 (b):x 非零时 ||x|| > 0

The absolute value, and in the complex case the modulus, is produced by this second extraction, which is why the identity reads |c| and not c.

name_en: Properties (a), (b), (c) follow at once from the axioms; only (d) needs proof

name_en: Property (d): the triangle inequality ||x + y|| <= ||x|| + ||y||

name_en: The conjugate in (15.11) comes from Hermitian symmetry, not from homogeneity
name_zh: (15.11) 中的共轭来自 Hermite 对称,而非齐次性
statement: Tracing the conjugate precisely: pairing (15.10) with y in the first slot gives (x, y) = sum of (x, e_i)(e_i, y), where each c_i = (x, e_i) is extracted by homogeneity in the FIRST slot and no conjugate arises. The conjugate appears only at the last step, when (e_i, y) is rewritten as the conjugate of (y, e_i) by axiom (1'), so that the formula is expressed in the components of y rather than in reversed products. So (15.11)'s conjugate is a bookkeeping consequence of Hermitian symmetry, not of conjugate-homogeneity.

name_en: Norm form (15.12): ||x||^2 = sum of |(x, e_i)|^2
statement: Setting x = y in (15.11) gives ||x||^2 = sum over i of |(x, e_i)|^2. Two collapses happen at once: (x, e_i) times its own conjugate becomes the squared modulus, and (x, x) becomes ||x||^2 by the definition of the norm. This is the abstract Pythagorean theorem, and specialized to the normalized trigonometric system it is the classical Parseval identity for Fourier coefficients.

anchors.quote: When x = y, Equation (15.11) reduces to (15.12).

atomic_reason: One specialization by a single substitution x = y.
